newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jews trace Hebron roots to days of the Bible.
newsitem.headline: Jews trace Hebron roots to days of the Bible.

text.p: The Bible says that in Hebron some 4,000 years ago Abraham, father of the Jews, paid the substantial sum of 400 shekels of silver for a cave in which to bury his wife Sarah.
The Cave of Machpelah -- the tomb of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and their wives -- is one reason Hebron's 400 Jews say they can lay claim to the town of 100,000 Arabs.

Another is that some 3,000 years ago, the Bible says, King David made Hebron his capital for seven years before moving north to Jerusalem. The town is one of four ancient Jewish holy cities along with Jerusalem, Safed and Tiberias.
"For me the arrangement on Hebron is a hard thing because I have a deep connection to these (holy) places," Israel's right-wing leader Benjamin Netanyahu told the newspaper Haaretz.

Yet just as the settlers use the Bible to assert a God-given right to the whole of the town, others interpret the biblical account of Abraham buying the land from Ephron the Hittite to mean the town clearly belonged to someone other than the Jews.
About 2,000 years ago King Herod the Great built a wall around the Tomb of the Patriarchs still admired for its beauty and engineering and the enormity of its stone blocks.
Hebron came under Byzantine, Arab, Crusader, Mameluke, Ottoman, British, Jordanian, and Israeli rule. The town drew religious scholars to visit a site sacred to Jews, Moslems and Christians.
A hospital was built about 100 years ago and named Beit Hadassah for the women's Zionist organisation whose medical staff offered free care to Arabs and Jews.
By 1929, under British rule, Hebron's Jews numbered 700, according to the Encyclopaedia Judaica.

In August of that year Arab rioters, opposed to rising Jewish immigration and inflamed by sermons at local mosques, massacred 67 men, women and children in Hebron. They wounded scores of people, razed buildings and destroyed Torah scrolls.

To this day Jews complain the British did not intervene to stop the riots. Over the next few years Jews tried to rebuild Hebron but renewed Arab riots in 1936 prompted the British authorities to evacuate the Jewish community.

Jordan held the town from 1948, the year Britain left, until the 1967 Middle East war when Israel captured it with the rest of the West Bank. The old Jewish quarter was found destroyed, the cemetery nearly wiped out.

Hebron was home to 40,000 Arabs, most of them Moslems, when in 1968, Jews led by Rabbi Moshe Levinger rented a small hotel and announced they would resettle the town despite opposition from both Arabs and Jews.

After three weeks the group moved to Hebron military headquarters where they lived until the founding of the adjacent Kiryat Arba Jewish settlement in 1971. Kiryat Arba gave birth in 1973 to what became Gush Emunim (the Bloc of the Faithful), militantly devoted to settling the biblical Land of Israel.

In 1979 a group of women and children secretly broke into long deserted Beit Hadassah. Under siege, they lived for a year in crude conditions. Finally in response to Arab attacks and after negotiations and protests, Prime Minister Menachem Begin's right-wing government allowed them to stay.

The town, a stronghold also for Moslem militants opposed to peace moves, has a history steeped in religion -- and blood. Levinger once killed an Arab bystander during a shooting rampage after Arabs stoned his car. Israel jailed him for a few months.

In 1980 Arab gunmen killed six Jews on their way home from a synagogue. Israel expelled the mayors of Hebron and neighbouring Halhoul, accusing them of incitement. In 1983, masked Jews killed three Arab students and wounded more than 30 in a machinegun attack at the Islamic College in Hebron.
In February 1994, Kiryat Arba settler Baruch Goldstein massacred 29 Palestinians kneeling in prayer at al-Ibrahimi mosque before survivors beat him to death.
Jews of Hebron say they would expand their community but the Israeli government prevents them from buying property and limits them to building only in existing Jewish neighbourhoods.
The fate of the Jews in Hebron and in other West Bank settlements will be decided in "final-status" talks between Israel and the Palestinians due to be completed by May 1999.
